m1.buyer.a1.action: As a Habitual App User, if my usual mobile order time slot is unavailable, I will accept a new pickup time if it's within an 8-minute delay. If this happens more than twice in a week, or the delay is longer, I will try the app for a nearby Dunkin' or Dutch Bros.

m1.buyer.a2.action: As a Commuter, if the Starbucks app shows my order will be delayed at all, I will immediately abandon it. My time is too tight. I will check if a competitor is on my direct route for a faster option; otherwise, I will skip buying coffee altogether to ensure I'm not late for work.

m1.buyer.a3.action: As a Café Visitor, I will continue to go inside to order. I am hopeful this new policy will make my experience better by reducing the crowd and shortening the line for in-person service.

m1.dunkin.a1.action: Launch a local opt-in morning bundle offer in the 15 consenting franchise stores near pilot cafés for January 2027.

m1.dunkin.a2.action: Bundle includes a $6 breakfast Meal Deal targeting coffee-and-food value shoppers, promoted via the Dunkin app with advance ordering and rewards.

m1.dunkin.a3.action: Monitor basket contribution, repeat visits, and staffing costs carefully to ensure economics remain positive.

m1.dunkin.a4.action: Implement stop rules to exit any store where the offer reduces profitability or cannibalizes full-price sales.

m1.dunkin.a5.action: Coordinate shared local marketing emphasizing value and convenience to compete with Starbucks’ mobile pickup slots.

m1.dutch.a1.action: Launch a geo-fenced digital advertising campaign targeting areas around the 12 Dutch Bros shops during weekday peak hours (7-10 a.m.) in January 2027. The campaign will highlight 'Skip the Wait, Grab Your Dutch Bros!' and promote Order Ahead. Offer a $1 credit for first-time Order Ahead users making a purchase during this peak window.

m1.dutch.a2.action: Proactively adjust staffing schedules at the 12 shops to ensure optimal coverage and maximize throughput during weekday peak hours (7-10 a.m.) in January 2027. Communicate Order Ahead benefits through existing app channels and in-store signage to reinforce speed and convenience.

m1.home.a1.action: Implement capacity-aware mobile pickup slots in 50 pilot cafés during weekday peak (07:00–10:00) for January 2027, reserving 20% of measured 15-minute production capacity for in-café orders and offering later mobile pickup times when allocation is full.

m1.home.a2.action: Instrument and monitor all order attempts (mobile and café), offered pickup slots, completed orders, refunds, and incremental staffing hours in both pilot and 50 comparison cafés. Begin building paired-store and customer cohort data for baseline and intervention measurement.

board.evidence_status: Public research through 2026-09-12. Future actions and outcomes are a model simulation. No actual pilot store or customer records are supplied.
board.measurement_rule: Null means unmeasured. Keep real measurement fields null and complete observed sample counts at zero without sourced operating records. Put hypothetical estimates in separately named simulated_* fields with assumptions, never in observed fields. Maintain a concise public_strategy_history of observable implemented actions and consequences so later players can adapt. Do not publish private budgets, dossiers or unseen internal intentions. Advance calendar_period to the end of the current month.
board.public_market_context: Starbucks is investing in coffeehouse service, staffing and Smart Queue while US transactions are growing. Dutch Bros offers drive-through beverages and Order Ahead at participating shops. Dunkin offers coffee-and-food value and mobile ordering through a franchise network. Some morning purchases can shift to home preparation or disappear. Local overlaps and customer segments in this exercise are assumptions.

criteria.condition: The baseline-adjusted reduction in peak café order-to-handoff p90 wait is less than 20 percent by move two across at least forty complete pilot/comparison store pairs
criteria.observable: adjusted_cafe_wait_reduction_pct; equally weighted store-pair changes in p90 wait, comparing peak weekday windows before and after the pilot; complete_store_pairs >= 40
criteria.threshold: Below 20% reduction; fewer than 40 complete pairs or missing baseline/wait evidence is unevaluated

criteria.condition: Adjusted daily contribution per pilot café after lost orders, substitution between channels and incremental staffing is negative by move three across at least forty complete store pairs
criteria.observable: incremental_daily_contribution_usd after matched-store baseline adjustment, including all channels and added labor; complete_store_pairs >= 40
criteria.threshold: Below $0 per café per day; incomplete transaction or cost evidence is unevaluated

criteria.condition: Thirty-day repeat purchase among baseline mobile customers falls by more than three percentage points relative to the comparison-cohort change by move three
criteria.observable: mobile_repeat_change_pp; compare baseline-defined cohorts across all Starbucks purchase channels, with at least 1000 customers per arm and complete 30-day follow-up
criteria.threshold: Below -3 percentage points; incomplete cohorts or missing follow-up is unevaluated

decision.launch_period: January 2027; a proposed experiment, not an announced Starbucks policy
decision.offer: Capacity-aware mobile pickup slots with a protected café-order allocation from 7–10 a.m. on weekdays
decision.pricing: Keep beverage prices unchanged; assumed $3 contribution per incremental or lost transaction before added staffing, not a reported company figure
decision.scope: 50 pilot cafés and 50 comparison cafés; reserve 20% of measured 15-minute capacity for café orders at peak; no automatic transfer of the policy to other stores
decision.segment: 50 US company-operated cafés with nearby Dutch Bros and Dunkin alternatives, paired with 50 comparison cafés
decision.statement: Pilot peak-time mobile-order admission limits in 50 US Starbucks cafés during January–March 2027, reserving 20% of measured production capacity for café orders and offering later pickup slots when the mobile allocation is full.

capabilities: Choose a brand, channel, later time, home preparation or no purchase based on the public offer (b2, b7, b8).
State contingent choices separately for commuters, habitual app users and café visitors, without inventing population shares (b3, b4, b5, b6).
constraints: Each occasion has its own explicit time and spending ceiling; do not average them into a universal customer (b4, b5, b6).
No measured segment weights, switching probability or real participant testimony exists (b1, b3, b8).

facts.claim: Reported category context: NCA’s June 2026 report says 47% of American adults consumed specialty coffee in the past day. Among past-day specialty drinkers, 36% had coffee prepared outside the home, versus 23% among traditional coffee drinkers. These national aggregates are not local switching probabilities.
sources: https://www.ncausa.org/newsroom/Specialty-Coffee-Consumption-Remains-at-Record-High

facts.claim: Reported choices: Dutch Bros Order Ahead is available at participating shops; Dunkin offers app ordering and rewards. A credible alternative depends on the particular route and location, not merely national brand availability.
sources: https://www.dutchbros.com/order-ahead/

facts.claim: Assumed character: This player is a composite of morning purchase occasions, not a single person controlling the market and not a recruited survey panel. It may describe different segment choices but may not report votes or measured percentages.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed commuter occasion: A weekday commuter buys before a fixed work start, has 10 minutes of discretionary travel-and-wait time, and an $8 coffee-and-light-breakfast ceiling. A 4-minute detour consumes real slack. These figures are illustrative constraints, not survey findings.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed habitual-app occasion: A repeat Starbucks buyer values a familiar customization and prepaid ordering, allows an 8-minute pickup delay when communicated before paying, and may switch temporarily after two unreliable mornings. Loyalty friction exists, but its monetary value and prevalence are unknown.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed café occasion: A customer intends to sit for 25 minutes before a meeting and has a $7 drink budget. Predictable handoff and an available place to sit matter; a cheap drive-through is not a complete substitute for this occasion.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed outside option and household economics: Some mornings the customer can prepare coffee at home using an illustrative $1 marginal ingredient cost; time, preparation equipment and taste differ. Skipping the purchase or buying later is permissible. These examples do not establish local market shares.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed information rights: Customers see quoted pickup times, prices, offers, public store conditions and their own experience. They do not know confidential staffing plans, rivals’ margins, adjudicator confidence, or other customers’ behavior. No segment weights or demand elasticity have been measured.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

incentives: Minimize the total cost of the actual occasion: spending, detour, waiting and risk of being late (b4, b5, b6).
Preserve an enjoyable and reliable routine, with home preparation and postponement as real alternatives (b5, b7).
red_lines: Do not claim to have interviewed customers or treat model choices as observed demand (b3).
Do not read private competitor dossiers or claim that a national consumption statistic predicts local churn (b1, b8).

capabilities: Design an opt-in morning bundle or app offer with local stop rules and cost accounting (k3, k5, k6).
Measure basket contribution and repeat visits after discounts expire (k7, k8).
constraints: Only the 15 consenting stores are controllable; the group cannot impose a national price (k5).
The $20,000 monthly envelope includes incentives and staffing; actual unit margins remain unknown (k2, k6).
No inferred access to competitors’ customer records or automatic corporate reimbursement (k8).

facts.claim: Reported history and footprint: Founded in 1950, Dunkin describes more than 14,000 restaurants in nearly 40 markets. Its franchise footprint and routine coffee-and-food occasion provide a different operating model from a company-run café pilot.
sources: https://www.dunkindonuts.com/about-us/

facts.claim: Reported ownership and transaction economics: Inspire completed the acquisition of Dunkin Brands in December 2020 in a transaction valued at $11.3 billion including assumed debt. That figure is an acquisition value for Dunkin Brands, not Dunkin revenue, available cash or franchisee profit. Current local margins are not supplied.
sources: https://inspirebrands.com/inspire-brands-completes-acquisition-of-dunkin-brands/

facts.claim: Reported commercial capability: The Dunkin app supports advance ordering, rewards and offers. Consumer terms and participation vary; app capability alone does not demonstrate shorter queues.
sources: https://www.dunkindonuts.com/en/mobile-app

facts.claim: Reported positioning: A September 2026 campaign advertised a $6 breakfast Meal Deal. It supplies evidence of a coffee-and-food value proposition; neither that January 2027 price nor universal franchise participation is assumed.
sources: https://news.dunkindonuts.com/blog/ttailgate-season-runs-on-dunkin-september2026

facts.claim: Assumed authority: The player represents a consenting local group of 15 franchised restaurants near some pilot cafés. It can coordinate a local opt-in offer and shared marketing but cannot order all US franchisees to participate. No new sites within three months.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed finances: Combined incremental local promotion and staffing spend is capped at $20,000 per month. For a proposed $1 discount, test a $2–$4 pre-discount contribution range; these are illustrative sensitivities, not disclosed unit economics. Franchise operators bear local labor and discount costs unless an explicit reimbursement is budgeted.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed backstory: The operator group has disagreed over prior offer redemptions that brought traffic without profitable food attachment. Its immediate priority is a repeatable breakfast basket and predictable pickup, with an explicit exit for stores whose economics worsen. This is a constructed governance tension.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed information rights: Participating stores can see their own basket mix, discount cost, staffing and repeat rewards visits, and public competitor offers. They cannot see Starbucks’ mobile customer identity or confidential café capacity. National campaign coordination and franchisor reimbursement are not granted.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

incentives: Win the whole breakfast occasion through a predictable, attractive coffee-and-food basket (k3, k4).
Keep participating franchisees economically willing to continue; redemption alone is not profit (k5, k6, k7).
red_lines: Do not describe acquisition value as operating revenue or promotion funding (k2).
Do not claim a local discount works without accounting for full-price purchases that would have occurred anyway (k6, k7).

capabilities: Run a geographically limited app offer and shift labor toward a measurable morning bottleneck (d4, d5).
Measure redeemed offers and subsequent full-price visits in the own-brand cohort (d8).
constraints: 12 shops, a $30,000 monthly incremental envelope and no new construction within the game (d5, d6).
Order Ahead availability is location-dependent; there is no measured spare capacity or proven local acquisition cost (d4, d6).
Public observation does not reveal individual rejected Starbucks customers (d8).

facts.claim: Reported history: Brothers Dane and Travis Boersma founded Dutch Bros in Grants Pass, Oregon, in 1992. The brand grew from an espresso pushcart around beverages and personal service; drive-through convenience is central to its operating identity.
sources: https://investors.dutchbros.com/overview/

facts.claim: Reported financials: Q2 2026 total revenue was $550.9 million, up 32.5% from $415.8 million. Company-operated same-shop sales grew 8.3%, including 3.4% transaction growth. Company revenue and company-operated comparable sales are distinct measures.
sources: https://investors.dutchbros.com/financials/quarterly-results/

facts.claim: Reported expansion: Dutch Bros opened 48 shops in Q2 2026, 44 company-operated. Inference: managers must preserve existing-shop execution while allocating staff and attention to growth. This does not establish spare local capacity.
sources: https://investors.dutchbros.com/financials/quarterly-results/

facts.claim: Reported capability: Dutch Bros offers app-based Order Ahead at participating shops. Pickup availability varies by location. This does not establish that every location in a hypothetical pilot market supports the feature.
sources: https://www.dutchbros.com/order-ahead/

facts.claim: Assumed local remit: The player controls 12 participating company-operated shops near some of the Starbucks pilot cafés. It can adjust shifts, app messaging and local acquisition offers, but cannot open a new shop within the three-round horizon.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed commercial envelope: Maximum incremental acquisition and labor budget $30,000 across these 12 shops per month. A $1 trial credit is a permitted option, not a precommitted action. Local variable contribution, queue capacity and cohort acquisition cost are unknown and must be estimated or measured before scaling.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed backstory: A regional operator has spent the preceding quarter integrating new staff and protecting service consistency. The local team wants repeat demand, not a one-week promotion that overwhelms the lane. This managerial history is scenario design, not reported company information.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed information rights: The operator sees its own lane times, app orders, rewards redemptions and repeat visits; it sees public Starbucks slot availability and public offers. It cannot target a verified list of customers rejected inside Starbucks’ app or read either rival’s private budget.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

incentives: Turn frustrated morning demand into repeat visits while protecting the service proposition (d1, d4).
Make existing-shop growth durable as expansion absorbs managerial capacity (d2, d3, d7).
red_lines: Do not assume every lost Starbucks order becomes a Dutch Bros order (d8).
Do not subsidize demand beyond the monthly envelope or promise a pickup time unsupported by local throughput (d6, d7).

capabilities: Use existing sequencing and staffing practices as the implementation base (h4).
Offer honest later pickup times, test narrower reservation windows and release unused capacity within the pilot (h5).
Build paired-store measurement, attempt-to-purchase funnels and baseline cohorts using internal instrumentation (h8, h9).
constraints: The two-hour staff allowance, unchanged prices and 50-store limit are binding game constraints (h5).
Segment margin is not a local cost curve; no store p90 waits or mobile churn elasticity is known (h2, h6, h8).
A booked later slot is not revenue until a purchase completes; competitor substitution is only partly observable (h8).

facts.claim: Reported history: Starbucks began in Seattle in 1971. Its evolution from a bean merchant into a coffeehouse makes the in-store experience part of the proposition, not simply a distribution expense. The strategic implication is an author inference.
sources: https://about.starbucks.com/about-us/

facts.claim: Reported financials: Q3 fiscal 2026 North America revenue was $7,395.1 million, operating income $1,008.9 million and operating margin 13.6%. These are segment figures, not pilot-store unit economics.
sources: https://investor.starbucks.com/news/financial-releases/news-details/2026/Starbucks-Reports-Q3-Fiscal-Year-2026-Results/default.aspx

facts.claim: Reported demand: US comparable sales increased 7.9% and comparable transactions 4.2% in Q3 fiscal 2026. This case tests sustaining growth; it does not assume that current transactions are declining.
sources: https://investor.starbucks.com/news/financial-releases/news-details/2026/Starbucks-Reports-Q3-Fiscal-Year-2026-Results/default.aspx

facts.claim: Reported strategy: Back to Starbucks combines staffing and scheduling investment, Smart Queue order sequencing, and restoration of the coffeehouse experience. These capabilities are public; the proposed 20% reservation is not an announced policy.
sources: https://about.starbucks.com/press/2026/back-to-starbucks-two-year-anniversary/

facts.claim: Assumed operating authority: 50 pilot and 50 comparison company-operated cafés; weekdays 07:00–10:00; reserve 20% of measured 15-minute capacity for café orders. Price unchanged. Each pilot café may add at most two peak staff-hours per weekday. Rollback or narrower time windows are allowed; expansion beyond 50 is not.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed economics: $3 contribution per incremental or lost transaction before additional staffing. Assume fully loaded incremental labor costs $30/hour for sensitivity calculations. Two added hours cost $60/store/day and require 20 genuinely incremental transactions to break even before other costs. No actual store margins, baselines or demand elasticities are supplied.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed management problem: The operations lead is accountable for café service and labor spend; the digital lead for reliable pickup and repeat behavior; the finance lead for all-channel contribution. Optimizing one channel at another’s expense is not success. These are role tensions constructed for the game, not testimony from executives.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed information rights: The team can instrument its own order attempts, offered pickup slots, completed orders, refunds, staffing hours and baseline-linked repeat purchases; it cannot see rivals’ transaction logs or know where a rejected mobile user ultimately buys. Available instrumentation is a capability, not already collected evidence.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

facts.claim: Assumed decision rules: By round two seek at least a 20% adjusted café p90 wait reduction across 40 complete pairs. By round three require nonnegative daily contribution and no worse than a 3pp adjusted repeat decline with 1,000 complete customers per arm. Missing evidence cannot pass these gates.
sources: Author-designed simulation assumption, 2026-09-12; not a company disclosure or measured customer observation.

incentives: Restore a credible coffeehouse visit without sacrificing digital convenience (h1, h4).
Defend positive transaction momentum while earning back added labor through all-channel contribution (h2, h3, h6).
Make a reversible operational choice before the March decision deadline (h5, h9).
red_lines: Do not invent operating measurements or declare the economics gate passed from a better wait-time story alone (h6, h9).
Do not promise a national rollout or exceed the staffing cap (h5).

actions: As a Habitual App User, if my usual mobile order time slot is unavailable, I will accept a new pickup time if it's within an 8-minute delay. If this happens more than twice in a week, or the delay is longer, I will try the app for a nearby Dunkin' or Dutch Bros.

As a Commuter, if the Starbucks app shows my order will be delayed at all, I will immediately abandon it. My time is too tight. I will check if a competitor is on my direct route for a faster option; otherwise, I will skip buying coffee altogether to ensure I'm not late for work.
As a Café Visitor, I will continue to go inside to order. I am hopeful this new policy will make my experience better by reducing the crowd and shortening the line for in-person service.
expected_responses: We don't expect competitors like Dunkin' or Dutch Bros to make any major changes in response to this small-scale test. We assume their service will remain consistent. For us, their normal, predictable service will become more attractive if our Starbucks routine is disrupted. They may gain some of our business by simply continuing to operate as they always have, acting as a reliable alternative.
content.rationale: Our decisions are based entirely on the needs of our specific morning routine. For some of us, like commuters, every second counts, and the risk of being late for work is not worth any particular brand of coffee. Any friction or delay introduced by this new system will force an immediate change in our behavior. For others who are habitual app users, we have some loyalty and flexibility, but that patience is limited. A reliable routine is important, and if the app becomes unreliable, we'll look for alternatives. For those of us who come to the café for the experience, we see this change as a potential positive. We've been frustrated by the crowds of mobile-order customers, and if reserving capacity for us makes the visit more pleasant and predictable, we're more likely to keep coming back.
resource_commitments: Our daily coffee budget (around $7-$8) is not committed to any single company. It will go to whichever coffee shop—Starbucks, Dunkin', Dutch Bros, or another local spot—can meet our needs for speed, convenience, and experience on any given morning.
We are willing to spend a few minutes downloading and setting up a competitor's app if our primary choice becomes unreliable.

actions: Launch a local opt-in morning bundle offer in the 15 consenting franchise stores near pilot cafés for January 2027.
Bundle includes a $6 breakfast Meal Deal targeting coffee-and-food value shoppers, promoted via the Dunkin app with advance ordering and rewards.
Monitor basket contribution, repeat visits, and staffing costs carefully to ensure economics remain positive.
Implement stop rules to exit any store where the offer reduces profitability or cannibalizes full-price sales.
Coordinate shared local marketing emphasizing value and convenience to compete with Starbucks’ mobile pickup slots.
expected_responses: Starbucks may see some traffic shift toward Dunkin's value bundle, especially if Starbucks' mobile pickup slots limit café order capacity.
Dutch Bros may respond with adjustments to their drive-through offers or Order Ahead promotions to retain morning customers.
Franchisees will monitor profitability closely and may opt out if economics worsen, leading to potential scaling back of the offer.
Customers may appreciate the predictable value and convenience, increasing repeat visits if the offer is well executed.
content.rationale: Given Dunkin's strong franchise footprint and value positioning, a local opt-in bundle can attract and retain breakfast customers while controlling costs within the $20,000 monthly budget. The $6 Meal Deal aligns with recent advertising and leverages the Dunkin app capabilities to offer convenience without changing prices nationally. Careful measurement and stop rules protect franchisee economics amid competitive pressure from Starbucks’ capacity-aware mobile pickup pilot. This focused approach targets repeatable profitable transactions and predictable pickup during peak morning hours.
resource_commitments: Allocate up to $20,000 in combined local promotion and staffing costs for January 2027 across the 15 participating stores.
Use existing Dunkin app infrastructure for ordering and rewards without new technology investment.
Dedicate local marketing resources to promote the Meal Deal bundle and app usage in the pilot area.

actions: Launch a geo-fenced digital advertising campaign targeting areas around the 12 Dutch Bros shops during weekday peak hours (7-10 a.m.) in January 2027. The campaign will highlight 'Skip the Wait, Grab Your Dutch Bros!' and promote Order Ahead. Offer a $1 credit for first-time Order Ahead users making a purchase during this peak window.

Proactively adjust staffing schedules at the 12 shops to ensure optimal coverage and maximize throughput during weekday peak hours (7-10 a.m.) in January 2027. Communicate Order Ahead benefits through existing app channels and in-store signage to reinforce speed and convenience.
expected_responses: Starbucks: May observe a slight dip in mobile order volume or slower adoption of their new capacity management policy in the pilot stores, potentially attributing it to customer resistance or internal factors rather than direct competitor action.
Dunkin: Might intensify their own mobile ordering promotions or value offers if they notice increased morning traffic at Dutch Bros locations or anecdotal evidence of Starbucks customer frustration.

Customers: Some Starbucks customers, especially those inconvenienced by the new mobile order limits or longer wait times, will be attracted by Dutch Bros' convenience messaging and the $1 incentive, leading to trial. Those who experience fast, friendly service will likely become repeat customers.
content.rationale: Starbucks' new policy of limiting mobile order admissions and reserving capacity during peak morning hours creates an opportunity to capture customers seeking speed and convenience. Our core identity is built on drive-through convenience and personal service. By launching a targeted digital campaign with a trial incentive, we can attract potentially frustrated Starbucks customers to try Dutch Bros' Order Ahead and fast service. Simultaneously, optimizing staffing ensures that we deliver on our promise of speed and a positive experience, converting trial into durable repeat visits and protecting our service proposition, which is crucial for existing-shop growth while we continue to expand.
resource_commitments: Allocate $10,000 for digital advertising spend across the 12 shops for January 2027.
Cap the $1 Order Ahead credit at $10,000 for January 2027 (up to 10,000 redemptions).
Allocate up to $10,000 for incremental labor hours across the 12 shops for January 2027 to ensure peak-hour operational excellence.

actions: Implement capacity-aware mobile pickup slots in 50 pilot cafés during weekday peak (07:00–10:00) for January 2027, reserving 20% of measured 15-minute production capacity for in-café orders and offering later mobile pickup times when allocation is full.

Instrument and monitor all order attempts (mobile and café), offered pickup slots, completed orders, refunds, and incremental staffing hours in both pilot and 50 comparison cafés. Begin building paired-store and customer cohort data for baseline and intervention measurement.
expected_responses: Dutch Bros and Dunkin may emphasize their own digital ordering convenience or drive-through speed to attract mobile customers who are offered later Starbucks pickup slots.

Some Starbucks mobile customers may shift to in-café ordering, accept later pickup times, or defect to competitors, but the protected café allocation should improve the in-store experience and reduce peak wait times.
Competitors may test limited-time offers or value promotions to capture any displaced Starbucks demand but lack visibility into the pilot's internal measurement or results.
content.rationale: Protecting a portion of peak production capacity for café orders addresses the strategic need to restore the in-store coffeehouse experience (h1, h4) without sacrificing digital convenience. This operational experiment is designed to balance transaction growth (h3) and all-channel contribution (h6, h7), while remaining reversible and within the defined scope (h5). Instrumentation is essential to generate the evidence needed for later decision gates, since no actual store or customer measurements are yet available (h8, h9).
resource_commitments: Dedicate up to two additional staff-hours per weekday morning per pilot café to support the new order sequencing and customer flows, at an assumed cost of $60/store/day (h5, h6).
Deploy internal measurement and reporting tools to track attempt-to-purchase funnels, slot offers, completions, and staffing for both pilot and comparison cafés.
